newsitem.title: INDIA: India's Tata Electric Cos 1996/97 net seen down.
newsitem.headline: India's Tata Electric Cos 1996/97 net seen down.

text.p: A fall in power offtake and a hike in regional power prices will cut Tata Electric Companies' (TEC) 1996/97 (April-March) net profit, analysts said on Wednesday.

Analysts expected TEC's net 1996/97 profit to fall to average 3.1 billion rupees ($86.7 million) from 4.45 billion rupees last year. Sales were seen dropping to an average 22.8 billion rupees in 1996/97 from 23.40 billion rupees.

TEC is a composite of three power generating companies, Tata Power Ltd, Andhra Valley Power Supply Company Ltd and Tata Hydro Electricity Power Supply Co Ltd, that supply power to India's financial capital.

It is due to announce earnings announced on June 26. The composite sales and profits will split in a ratio of five-to-three-to-two, with the largest chunk to Tata Power and the smallest to Tata Hydro.

"TEC's unit sales of power are likely to drop about nine percent. One of its largest buyers, Bombay Suburban Electric Supply Ltd (BSES), has also ventured into power generation," said Rajesh Bharatkar, power analyst at Citicorp Securities and Investments Ltd.

He said BSES' commissioning of its 500 megawatt plant at Dahanu had reduced its dependency on TEC by 40 percent. Historically, BSES has purchased about 35 percent of TEC's power and distributed it to Bombay's suburbs.
Analysts said TEC's future growth prospects were not very positive and expected profits to stay flat.

"With BSES' purchases reduced and no large power intensive industry coming up around Bombay, TEC will be forced to sell power to the Maharashtra State Electricity Board (MSEB)," said an analyst at a leading French investment house.
He said MSEB's per kilowatt hour realisation is 1.70 rupees compared to BSES' 2.40 rupees.

He said TEC raised its power tariff with MSEB but failed to fully pass on the tariff to BSES. "The company has not been able to benefit fully from this power tariff hike, and this will impact its profits," he said.
Analysts said the company's lack of firm investment plans would also keep net 1997/98 profit flat despite an expected revenue rise.
They predicted TEC's net to stay around 3.2 billion rupee for 1997/98 as sales climb to an average 24.2 billion rupees.

"TEC will suffer until it can chart out a concrete investment plan. The status of its 450-megawatt project in Bhivpuri is unclear, as is that of its proposal to take over TISCO's plant near Jamshedpur," said an analyst at a leading Swiss bank.
